title: Your Brain Does Not See Everything
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Your Brain Does Not See Everything. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A passenger opens a travel app to check a departure time. A small banner at the top says the gate has changed, but the passenger's eye goes straight to the large departure card they came to read. The message was on the screen. It never became part of the decision. This lesson explains why being visible is not the same as being noticed, understood, and acted on.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Perception is selective and expectation-led. People do not inspect every pixel and then decide what matters. They notice a small subset of what is available, guided by their goal, prior knowledge, location of attention, contrast, motion, and what they expect a screen like this to contain. The rest is filtered, interpreted quickly, or missed entirely.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This is why an important message cannot be made reliable by merely placing it on a screen. It needs to be in the person's path, distinguishable from surrounding material, expressed in language they can understand, and timed when it can change the next action.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A bright element can attract attention but still fail if it looks like an ad, appears after the decision, or does not explain what to do.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we follow the attention filter step by step?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Goal and expectation → attention lands on a few cues → interpretation → action.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Imagine the screen has three competing elements: a large departure card, a small gate-change message, and a promotion. Someone checking the departure time is likely to start with the card. If the gate change sits outside that path, the person may act on an incomplete picture. The design question is not simply how bright to make the banner.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It is where the new information belongs in the task and what action it requires.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Mechanism: perception is an active prediction
turns.text: How does perception is an active prediction actually work?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Vision is not a complete recording that the mind inspects later. People direct their eyes through movements and brief fixations, while attention selects a fraction of available information for deeper processing. Top-down factors—goal, expectation, prior knowledge, and current question—make some signals likely to be sampled.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Bottom-up features—contrast, onset, motion, size, and novelty—can capture attention, but capture is not the same as correct interpretation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This distinction explains several apparently contradictory findings. A visually loud message can be ignored because it resembles advertising. A subtle change can be detected when it appears exactly where a person is monitoring. A person can look directly at an element without incorporating its meaning into the task.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Change blindness is especially likely when a change occurs during a transition or outside the attended object. Inattentional blindness occurs when attention is occupied by another demand. Neither is evidence that a person is careless.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Diagnose the missing stage. Did the eyes fail to reach the information? Was the signal seen but grouped as irrelevant? Was it read but misunderstood? Was it understood after the moment for action? Eye tracking may help with the first question but cannot answer all four. Combine brief exposure, observation, recall, comprehension, and action.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The design response should match the failure: placement for sampling, visual form for discrimination, language for meaning, timing for usefulness, and persistent state for later verification.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The boundary is important: making every critical item larger or animated creates competition and habituation. Salience must express a priority model. In high-consequence work, the system may need to block or restructure an action; visual emphasis alone is not a reliable safety control.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What would you do with that in a real product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Start with the one thing a person needs to notice at this moment. Remove or subordinate competing signals. Do not rely only on colour: use position, clear language, shape, and persistent status. Test the screen with a brief exposure, then ask what people saw and what they think it meant. If they cannot report the critical information, it did not function as a message.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Treat “nobody noticed it” as a diagnosis problem. Was the information absent from the task path? Did it resemble low-value content? Did the team's visual system make everything equally loud? Did the message arrive when it could no longer change behaviour? These hypotheses lead to different fixes and different measures.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Selective perception creates a gap between availability and usability. A person’s current goal, previous experience, location of attention, expectations, and environmental distraction determine what becomes meaningful. Salience can attract a glance, but relevance and timing determine whether that glance changes action.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Important information should be in the task path, distinguishable from low-value material, understandable at a glance, and present while the person can still respond.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test perception rather than assuming it from implementation. Use brief-exposure studies, task observation, comprehension checks, and behavioural signals to see whether a message was noticed and correctly understood. Consider accessibility too: an alert conveyed only by colour, animation, or visual location may not reach everyone.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The system needs redundant, appropriate cues matched to consequence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Technically present: a critical message exists but looks like advertising or background chrome. Too-late signal: information appears after the person can no longer alter their choice. Single-cue dependency: colour, motion, or position is the only way to perceive a meaningful change. Signal competition: every message uses the same urgency treatment, so none is credible.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a travel app. A time-sensitive gate change appears in a slim banner while the main departure card continues to show the old gate. A passenger who checks only the card leaves with the wrong information. A stronger design updates the card itself, makes the change distinguishable, and gives the passenger a way to confirm the current gate.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This is a hypothetical example, not a claim about a particular app.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 1 taught that an experience is an attempt to make progress. This lesson explains why a correct interface response can still fail to become part of that attempt. lesson 8 will show how grouping and hierarchy make the intended information easier to perceive.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Open a dense screen for three seconds. Close it and list what you noticed, what you missed, and what you assumed was important. Compare that with what the product actually needed you to do.
